oneLineAnswer: Famotidine is an acid reducer sold by prescription and over the counter for heartburn, ulcers and reflux.
whatItIs: Famotidine is an acid reducer. It is sold both by prescription and over the counter. It belongs to a drug group called histamine-2 receptor antagonists, often shortened to H2 blockers. The label lists its chemical formula as C8H15N7O2S3 and its molecular weight as 337.45.
whatItDoes: It lowers how much acid your stomach makes.
It blocks histamine-2 receptors, which cuts both the strength and the volume of stomach acid.
Prescription forms are approved for stomach ulcers, duodenal ulcers, reflux disease, and rare acid-overproduction conditions.
Over-the-counter tablets are meant for heartburn caused by acid indigestion and sour stomach.
The over-the-counter label says a tablet taken before trigger foods or drinks can prevent heartburn.
howPeopleUseIt: Many people take one occasionally for heartburn after a heavy, spicy or fatty meal, or after alcohol.
Others take it on a schedule, prescribed by a clinician, while an ulcer or reflux disease is being treated.
The over-the-counter label caps adults at two tablets in 24 hours and says children under 12 should ask a doctor.
Prescription tablets are approved for people weighing 40 kg or more, including children in that weight range.
People who took ranitidine before 2020 often moved to famotidine after the FDA pulled ranitidine from the market.

commonSideEffects: In trials, the most common reactions were headache, dizziness, constipation and diarrhea.
Headache, dizziness and constipation each showed up in at least 1% of people given famotidine.
Less common trial reports included nausea, vomiting, fatigue, dry mouth and muscle aches.
Approved labels also list rare reports of liver enzyme rises, low platelets and skin itching, gathered after the drug reached the market.
seriousSigns: The label warns that confusion, hallucinations, agitation and seizures have been reported, mainly in older adults and people with kidney problems.
Rare postmarketing reports include a severe allergic reaction called anaphylaxis, plus swelling of the face and hives.
Very rare skin reactions such as toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome have been reported after approval.
Heart rhythm problems, including a longer QT interval on an ECG, have been reported rarely.
The over-the-counter label says to stop and see a doctor if heartburn continues or gets worse, or if you need the product for more than 14 days.
The over-the-counter label lists trouble or pain swallowing food, vomiting blood, or bloody or black stools as signs of a serious condition worth a doctor visit.
whoShouldAvoid: Do not use famotidine if you have had a serious allergic reaction to it or to another H2 blocker.
The over-the-counter label says not to combine it with other acid reducers.
The over-the-counter label says to ask a doctor first if you have kidney disease, or heartburn lasting more than 3 months.
Older adults and people with kidney impairment are at higher risk of nervous-system effects, and labels note that dose adjustment is recommended.
The over-the-counter label says pregnant or breastfeeding people should ask a health professional before use.
Labels flag chest pain, shoulder pain, shortness of breath, sweating or unexplained weight loss alongside heartburn as reasons to see a doctor rather than self-treat.

interactions: Because famotidine reduces stomach acid, it can lower absorption of some other drugs and make them work less well.
The label says not to take it with dasatinib, delavirdine mesylate, cefditoren or fosamprenavir.
Other acid-sensitive drugs named in the label include atazanavir, erlotinib, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ledipasvir/sofosbuvir, nilotinib and rilpivirine.
Famotidine is considered a weak inhibitor of the liver enzyme CYP1A2 and may raise blood levels of tizanidine.
High tizanidine levels can cause low blood pressure, a slow heart rate or heavy drowsiness, so the label says to avoid the pair.
The over-the-counter label says to ask a doctor or pharmacist first if you take any prescription drug.
pregnancyAndChildren: Human pregnancy data are too limited to set a risk level. Animal studies found no clear harm at very high multiples of the human dose. The label says to use it during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Small amounts pass into rat milk, and human milk data are limited but showed no effects on the breastfed infant. There are no data on whether it affects milk production. Safety and effectiveness are established for ulcers and reflux in children. The 20 mg and 40 mg tablets are not recommended for children weighing under 40 kg.
whatWeDoNotKnow: The label states that available pregnancy data are insufficient to establish a drug-related risk of birth defects, miscarriage or other outcomes.
There are no human data on whether famotidine changes milk production.
The LiverTox page on drug-induced liver injury could not be loaded, so this record makes no claim about rare liver injury.
No source we reached gives long-term safety data for healthy people who take famotidine regularly for heartburn.
ClinicalTrials.gov shows ongoing research into other possible uses, such as burn scar itch, but no results are posted for those.
We did not find a fetched source describing how many people use famotidine for any unapproved purpose.

No dose, schedule or personal protocol is stated here, by design; only what labels and studies recorded is reported, attributed.
No fetched source quantifies how many people take famotidine for unapproved uses.

Human breast-milk data are described by the label as limited, and milk-production effects are unstudied.
summary: This record covers what famotidine is, how it blocks stomach acid, its prescription and over-the-counter uses, its trial and postmarketing side effects, its labeled drug interactions, and the pregnancy, breastfeeding and pediatric gaps the label itself flags.
